title: Stacking layers: receptive fields & over-smoothing
blurb: K-hop receptive field, why embeddings collapse

hook.title: Overlapping address books
hook.text: Every node's embedding is built from the nodes in its **address book**: everyone within $K$ hops. Two people with completely different address books form different opinions. But as $K$ grows, address books balloon and overlap; two people who mostly hear from the *same crowd* end up with the *same opinion*. Stack enough layers and **everyone's opinion converges**, making it impossible to tell nodes apart. That is **over-smoothing**.
hook.recall: Remember the overlapping address books: more layers ⇒ larger, overlapping receptive fields ⇒ similar embeddings ⇒ over-smoothing. We need embeddings to *differentiate* nodes.

explore.intro: A path graph; the receptive field of a node after $K$ layers is its $K$-hop neighbourhood.
tasks: Keep nodes $a=4$ and $b=9$ fixed and raise $K$ from 0 to 8. When do their fields first overlap?
Move $a$ and $b$ close together. What happens to the overlap fraction?
explore.takeaway: Receptive field = nodes that determine a node’s embedding; in a $K$-layer GNN it is the $K$-hop neighbourhood. Many layers ⇒ highly overlapping fields ⇒ over-smoothing.

items: Nodes get highly overlapping receptive fields
build.explanation: Logic: stack many GNN layers → nodes will have highly overlapped receptive fields → node embeddings will be highly similar → over-smoothing.

options: All node embeddings converge to the same value
questions.explanation: Bad because we want embeddings to *differentiate* nodes.

questions.prompt: In a $K$-layer GNN, each node’s receptive field is:
questions.explanation: The set of nodes that determine the embedding of the node of interest.

questions.prompt: In a long **path graph**, how many nodes are in the receptive field of an interior node after $K=3$ layers (itself plus everything within 3 hops on both sides)?
questions.explanation: $2K+1=7$ for a path (derived by counting; the slide defines the field as the $K$-hop neighbourhood).

options: Adding more GNN layers does not always help (unlike CNNs for image classification)
Shared neighbours grow quickly when the number of layers increases
Highly overlapping receptive fields give highly similar embeddings
Over-smoothing is desirable because we want all embeddings to be equal
questions.explanation: We want embeddings to differentiate nodes; over-smoothing destroys that.

questions.prompt: *“To capture long-range information I should always set the number of GNN layers $L$ as large as possible.”* What’s wrong?
options: Don’t set $L$ unnecessarily large: more layers can cause over-smoothing; unlike CNNs, adding GNN layers doesn’t always help

questions.prompt: Why do two nodes with highly overlapped receptive fields get similar embeddings?
options: Each embedding is determined by its receptive field
They always have the same label
